anatomy.lede: A sea walnut is a living bag of seawater with eight shimmering rows of paddles, two big feeding lobes and a balance organ at the top.

hotspots.label: Comb row
hotspots.text: Eight rows of comb plates, each made of fused cilia, beat in waves to row the animal along. They scatter light into rainbows.

hotspots.label: Rainbow combs
hotspots.text: The colours are diffracted light from the beating plates, not the animal's own glow, and they vanish in darkness.

hotspots.label: Oral lobe
hotspots.text: Two large lobes flank the mouth. Lobate comb jellies, the group this species belongs to, are named after them.

hotspots.label: Second lobe
hotspots.text: The lobes are among the features lost when a stressed adult reverts to its two-tentacled larval form.

hotspots.label: Aboral end
hotspots.text: At the end opposite the mouth sits the aboral organ, a sensory hub with a gravity-sensing statocyst.

hotspots.label: Clear body
hotspots.text: The body is about 97% water, which makes it almost invisible in the sea.

senses.lede: With no brain and no eyes, a comb jelly still knows which way is up and can sense light.

senses.name: Statocyst
senses.text: Four clusters of ciliated 'balancer' cells hold up a tiny weight called the statolith. When the animal tilts, the load on the balancers shifts and changes how the comb rows beat, turning it back on course.

senses.name: Light-sensing cells
senses.text: Mnemiopsis has three opsin genes, which make light-detecting proteins. Opsins are active in its apical sensory organ and in the cells that make light.

senses.name: Seeing its own light?
senses.text: One opsin absorbs light at wavelengths that overlap with the animal's own blue-green glow, raising the idea that light production and light sensing are linked.

body.lede: Comb jellies belong to one of the oldest branches of the animal tree, and their bodies work in ways found nowhere else.

systems.title: A fused nerve net
systems.text: Electron microscopy showed that neurons in its nerve net share one continuous cell membrane, forming a syncytium rather than separate cells linked by synapses.

systems.title: Light from a protein
systems.text: Its genome holds 10 full-length photoprotein genes, the light-making proteins in its photocytes, which line canals running through the body.

systems.title: Rebuilding the body
systems.text: A sea walnut can regenerate any missing organ, and can regrow a whole body from a fragment as small as about 15% of the original in a few days.

genome.lede: Mnemiopsis was the first comb jelly to have its genome sequenced, and the result reshaped ideas about the earliest animals.

findings.title: Sister to all other animals?
findings.text: The 2013 genome analysis suggested that comb jellies, not sponges, are the sister group of all other animals.

findings.title: Muscles invented twice?
findings.text: Mnemiopsis lacks many genes used by bilaterian muscle and other mesodermal cells, suggesting such cell types may have evolved independently in comb jellies.

findings.title: Thirteen chromosomes
findings.text: A 2025 chromosome-level assembly of about 248 million base pairs found 13 chromosomes and an unusual set of immune genes.

survival.lede: The sea walnut is a fragile animal that thrives through sheer numbers and flexibility.

tactics.title: Eating its own young
tactics.text: In the Baltic Sea, once adults have cleared the water of prey, they switch to eating their own larvae and keep building nutrient reserves for lean months.

tactics.title: Tough to kill
tactics.text: It tolerates salinity from 2 to 38 psu and temperatures from 2 to 32 °C.

tactics.title: Turning back time
tactics.text: Stressed adults can revert to the larval form and later grow up again, a possible way to ride out hard times.

life.lede: A sea walnut is hermaphroditic, so a single animal can fertilise its own eggs.

stages.name: Egg
stages.text: Spawning starts late in the evening or around 1–2 a.m. Eggs are released into the water, where they are fertilised.

stages.name: Cydippid larva
stages.text: The young hatch as rounded cydippid larvae with two tentacles, quite unlike the lobed adult.

stages.name: Lobate adult
stages.text: The larva grows lobes and becomes an adult. Egg-laying can begin at a body length of only about 15 mm.

stages.name: Reverse development
stages.text: Under stress, an adult can turn back into a cydippid larva, then mature and spawn again.
